title: ECG Interpretation: Rate, Rhythm, Intervals, Axis, Ischemia, Then the Patient
bottomLine: Read ECGs systematically and clinically: verify rate/rhythm, P waves, PR/QRS/QT, axis and ST-T pattern, then decide whether the tracing explains symptoms or represents a time-sensitive rhythm/ischemic/conduction problem. Never let an automated interpretation overrule an unstable patient or an obvious tracing abnormality.
recognize: Regularity, P-QRS relationship, QRS width and rate quickly narrow the rhythm differential.
Dynamic ST-T change, high-grade AV block, sustained ventricular arrhythmia or a markedly prolonged QT in the right context changes urgency.
differentiate: Sinus tachycardia has an underlying driver; SVT is a rhythm diagnosis.
Baseline repolarization abnormalities, paced rhythms and bundle-branch patterns can complicate ischemia interpretation and may require comparison or specialist review.
assessment: Start with symptoms and stability: chest pain, syncope, dyspnea, palpitations, electrolyte/drug exposure and hemodynamics.
Compare with prior ECG when available and verify lead placement when the pattern is unexpected.
workup: Use serial ECGs and troponin when acute ischemia is suspected; obtain electrolytes/drug levels or other testing according to the rhythm context.
Do not order an ECG as a ritual without a clinical question, but do not delay it in time-sensitive chest pain, syncope or arrhythmia.
management: Escalate unstable tachy/bradyarrhythmia, STEMI-equivalent or malignant ventricular rhythms according to acute-care protocols.
Stable incidental abnormalities need cause/risk review and appropriate follow-up rather than reflex emergency treatment.
medicationSafety: Review QT-prolonging and rate-slowing medications and electrolyte abnormalities when conduction/repolarization issues are present.
redFlags: ST-elevation/dynamic ischemic change with compatible symptoms
counselling: Explain that one ECG is a time sample; intermittent arrhythmia can require longer monitoring.
followUp: Ensure abnormal tracings are compared, interpreted and acted on rather than simply filed as 'abnormal ECG'.
examTrap: Accepting the machine label as the diagnosis without checking rhythm logic, intervals, ST-T changes and the patient's stability.
oneLinePearl: ECG interpretation is a sequence, not pattern-spotting: rhythm, conduction, ischemia, context.

title: Chest X-Ray: Answer the Clinical Question Without Overcalling the Image
bottomLine: Interpret chest radiography systematically—quality, airway, lungs/pleura, cardiac/mediastinal contours, diaphragms and devices—then correlate with symptoms. A normal chest x-ray does not exclude early ACS, PE, asthma or every pneumonia, and an incidental opacity is not automatically infection.
recognize: Focal air-space opacity, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, edema pattern, cardiomegaly and device malposition are high-yield findings.
Projection, rotation, inspiration and portable AP technique can distort heart size and apparent lung findings.
differentiate: Pulmonary edema, infection, atelectasis and hemorrhage can overlap radiographically and require clinical correlation.
PE is usually not diagnosed by chest x-ray; a normal film does not exclude it.
assessment: Know the indication, symptoms, oxygenation and prior imaging before interpreting a nonspecific finding.
workup: Use the chest x-ray to answer the first-line thoracic question; escalate to CT/ultrasound or other modality only when the clinical differential and CAR referral guidance justify it.
management: Act urgently on pneumothorax with instability, major edema, significant device malposition or another emergent finding.
Stable incidental findings require documented follow-up rather than unplanned repeat films.
medicationSafety: Do not start antibiotics solely from a nonspecific opacity without a compatible infectious syndrome.
redFlags: New large effusion with respiratory compromise
counselling: Explain when additional imaging is needed and when a chest x-ray is reassuring but not definitive for the suspected condition.
followUp: Own radiology recommendations for interval imaging or further characterization.
examTrap: Using a normal chest x-ray to rule out pulmonary embolism or ACS.
oneLinePearl: Read the film systematically, then ask whether it actually answers the patient's problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Radiologists Referral Guidelines

title: Abdominal Imaging: Ultrasound, CT, or Another Test Based on the Differential
bottomLine: Select abdominal imaging from the suspected pathology, urgency and patient context. Ultrasound is often first-line for biliary, pelvic and pregnancy-related questions; CT is high-yield for many acute intra-abdominal emergencies; MRI can solve selected soft-tissue/pregnancy/hepatobiliary questions when appropriate.
recognize: RUQ pain/jaundice, RLQ pain, obstruction/perforation concern, renal colic, pelvic pain and vascular catastrophe each require different imaging pathways.
Pregnancy and pediatrics increase the importance of avoiding unnecessary ionizing radiation while still imaging emergencies when needed.
differentiate: Screening ultrasound is not the same as diagnostic imaging for a symptomatic patient.
A negative test chosen for the wrong question is not reassuring.
assessment: Define pain location/onset, peritonitis, hemodynamics, pregnancy status, prior surgery, renal function and the leading dangerous alternatives.
workup: Use CAR referral guidance to choose ultrasound, CT, MRI or no imaging according to the clinical syndrome and pretest probability.
Do not order CT before basic bedside/laboratory evaluation when that information changes the imaging question.
management: Escalate suspected perforation, ischemia, ruptured aneurysm, ectopic pregnancy or obstructed infected system urgently; imaging should not create treatment delay when the patient is unstable.
medicationSafety: Contrast decisions require renal/hypersensitivity context; analgesia should not be withheld merely to preserve examination findings.
counselling: Explain why the selected modality fits the suspected disease and why another modality may be unnecessary.
followUp: Close the loop on incidental or indeterminate findings that need repeat or advanced imaging.
examTrap: Ordering the same CT abdomen for every abdominal pain syndrome regardless of pregnancy, biliary/pelvic question or pretest diagnosis.
oneLinePearl: Abdominal imaging starts with the differential, not the scanner.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Radiologists Referral Guidelines

title: Musculoskeletal Imaging: Image the Red Flag or the Management-Changing Question
bottomLine: Most uncomplicated musculoskeletal pain is diagnosed clinically and does not need immediate advanced imaging. Use x-ray for many fracture/degenerative questions, ultrasound for selected tendon/soft-tissue problems, and MRI for neurologic, marrow, occult-fracture or soft-tissue questions when the result will change management.
recognize: Trauma mechanism, inability to bear weight/use limb, deformity, focal bony tenderness, fever, cancer history or progressive neurologic deficit increase imaging value.
Low-back pain without red flags generally does not need early imaging.
differentiate: Degenerative changes on imaging are common and may not explain symptoms.
MRI is not automatically superior if the clinical question is a simple fracture or osteoarthritis pattern.
assessment: Perform focused joint/spine/neurovascular examination and apply validated clinical decision rules where appropriate before ordering imaging.
workup: Use CAR/Choosing Wisely referral guidance to select x-ray, ultrasound, CT or MRI based on the management-changing question.
management: Urgently image suspected fracture with neurovascular compromise, septic joint/osteomyelitis, cauda equina, malignancy or other red flags.
Manage uncomplicated mechanical pain conservatively first when guideline criteria support it.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary contrast/radiation and avoid delaying analgesia or stabilization while pursuing low-value imaging.
redFlags: Hot swollen joint with systemic illness
counselling: Explain that imaging often finds age-related changes that do not require intervention.
followUp: Image later if symptoms fail expected conservative recovery or new red flags develop.
examTrap: Ordering MRI immediately for uncomplicated acute low-back pain with no red flags.
oneLinePearl: Image when the result can change what you do next.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Radiologists Referral Guidelines
Choosing Wisely Canada Radiology recommendations updated 2026

title: Neuroimaging: Match CT, CTA, MRI, and Vascular Imaging to the Neurologic Syndrome
bottomLine: Neuroimaging is syndrome- and time-dependent. Acute stroke/hemorrhage, thunderclap headache, trauma and focal deficit have different CT/CTA/MRI pathways, while stable migraine or uncomplicated syncope often needs no routine brain imaging.
recognize: Noncontrast CT is rapid for acute hemorrhage/trauma; vascular imaging is essential for selected acute stroke/vascular syndromes; MRI is more sensitive for many parenchymal/posterior-fossa/inflammatory conditions.
Time from symptom onset and the treatment decision determine urgency and modality.
differentiate: A normal early CT does not exclude all ischemic stroke or every cause of thunderclap headache.
Routine imaging for stable typical migraine or uncomplicated syncope can create incidental findings without improving care.
assessment: Define exact onset/last-known-well, focal deficits, trauma, anticoagulation, seizure, fever, cancer/immunocompromise, pregnancy/postpartum and headache onset-to-peak.
workup: Use current CAR CNS referral guidance and stroke pathways to choose CT/CTA/MRI/MRA or no imaging.
Do not delay reperfusion/stabilization to pursue a nonessential outpatient-style workup.
management: Activate emergency stroke/neurosurgical pathways when imaging is time-critical; use outpatient MRI selectively for nonemergent structural/inflammatory questions.
medicationSafety: Contrast and sedation decisions require renal, allergy, pregnancy and airway considerations; thrombolysis decisions require the stroke team, not imaging interpretation alone.
counselling: Explain why some neurologic symptoms need immediate CT/vascular imaging while others do not benefit from routine scans.
followUp: Ensure incidental/indeterminate findings and recommended repeat imaging have explicit ownership.
examTrap: Ordering routine CT head for uncomplicated syncope or stable migraine while missing time-critical vascular imaging in acute focal stroke.
oneLinePearl: Neuroimaging is chosen by syndrome, timing, and the decision the image must support.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Radiologists CNS Referral Guidelines 2025

title: Ultrasound in Primary Care: Use a Focused Question, Know Its Blind Spots
bottomLine: Ultrasound is valuable when the clinical question fits its strengths—biliary, pelvic/obstetric, vascular, soft-tissue and selected bedside questions—but it is operator- and anatomy-dependent. A negative study does not exclude a disease the modality is poorly suited to detect.
recognize: Ultrasound avoids ionizing radiation and can be first-line in pregnancy/children for many indications.
Point-of-care ultrasound supports focused bedside decisions but does not replace a comprehensive diagnostic study when one is required.
differentiate: POCUS answers a narrow question such as free fluid, bladder retention or gross cardiac function; formal ultrasound provides a more comprehensive radiologic examination.
Obesity, bowel gas and deep/complex anatomy can limit diagnostic quality.
assessment: Define the question before ordering or scanning and know whether a negative result would genuinely change probability.
workup: Use CAR referral criteria and local scope/training standards to select formal ultrasound versus another modality.
management: Act on high-risk ultrasound findings within the clinical syndrome; escalate to CT/MRI/specialist review when the ultrasound is nondiagnostic and the dangerous differential remains.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary procedural sedation/contrast when ultrasound can answer the question; conversely, do not delay needed CT/MRI solely to avoid radiation when emergency diagnosis depends on it.
counselling: Explain that ultrasound's safety does not make it the right test for every problem.
followUp: Close the loop on limited/nondiagnostic studies and recommended follow-up imaging.
examTrap: Treating a negative limited ultrasound as proof that a poorly visualized dangerous condition is absent.
oneLinePearl: Ultrasound is powerful when the question matches the modality.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Radiologists Referral Guidelines
Canadian POCUS scope and imaging practice principles

title: CT: Use Speed and Anatomic Detail When the Benefit Justifies Radiation and Contrast Risk
bottomLine: CT is fast and excellent for many acute anatomic questions, but ionizing radiation and iodinated-contrast risks mean it should be selected by indication rather than convenience. Pregnancy, pediatrics, renal function, prior contrast reactions and whether contrast is actually necessary all modify the plan.
recognize: CT is high-yield for trauma, hemorrhage, many acute abdominal/thoracic conditions and selected vascular studies.
Noncontrast and contrast-enhanced CT answer different questions; adding contrast routinely can reduce rather than improve diagnostic value for some indications.
differentiate: Radiation is not an absolute contraindication when CT is needed for a life-threatening diagnosis, including in pregnancy.
Renal dysfunction and previous contrast reaction require risk mitigation/alternatives, not reflex cancellation of every contrast study.
assessment: Clarify indication, urgency, pregnancy, renal function, contrast reaction history and previous imaging.
workup: Use CAR referral guidance to choose protocol and whether contrast is required; avoid duplicate CT when recent adequate imaging already answers the question.
management: Proceed when expected diagnostic benefit outweighs risk and use radiology consultation for protocol/contrast uncertainty.
medicationSafety: Follow current CAR/CSACI contrast-hypersensitivity guidance rather than outdated blanket premedication rules.
Review metformin/renal and other medication considerations according to current contrast policy.
redFlags: Other unstable conditions where delay is harmful
counselling: Explain radiation/contrast risk in proportion to the clinical benefit rather than using fear-based counselling.
followUp: Own incidental findings and recommended follow-up rather than repeating CT without a plan.
examTrap: Avoiding a clinically necessary CT in an unstable pregnant patient solely because radiation is involved.
oneLinePearl: CT is justified by the question and urgency, then optimized for radiation and contrast safety.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Radiologists Referral Guidelines

title: MRI: Tissue Detail Without Ionizing Radiation, but Not Without Safety Screening
bottomLine: MRI provides excellent soft-tissue, neurologic, MSK and cardiovascular characterization without ionizing radiation, but safety depends on implant/device screening, ability to tolerate the scan and whether gadolinium is needed. MRI is not automatically the 'best' test when CT or ultrasound answers the question faster or more appropriately.
recognize: MRI is particularly useful for CNS, marrow/soft tissue, selected hepatobiliary/pelvic disease and cardiac tissue characterization.
2026 CAR pregnancy guidance supports indication-based MRI safety while keeping gadolinium use appropriately restricted/justified.
differentiate: Many modern implants are MRI-conditional rather than absolutely contraindicated, but exact device conditions must be verified.
MRI's lack of radiation does not justify delaying time-critical CT in acute hemorrhage/trauma or other emergencies.
assessment: Screen for implanted devices/metal, pregnancy, severe claustrophobia, ability to lie still, renal function if gadolinium is considered and urgency.
workup: Use CAR referral guidelines and radiology input to choose MRI sequence/contrast and determine whether another modality is more appropriate.
management: Use MRI when tissue characterization or radiation avoidance materially changes diagnosis/management; refer device-conditional or sedation-complex cases through the appropriate imaging pathway.
medicationSafety: Gadolinium decisions require current renal/pregnancy/product guidance; sedation requires airway and monitoring planning.
redFlags: Unknown high-risk implant/foreign body before scanning
Severe renal impairment when contrast is proposed without clear benefit
counselling: Explain that 'no radiation' does not mean 'no screening' and that MRI may take longer and require device/contrast planning.
followUp: Track significant incidental or indeterminate findings and recommended repeat imaging.
examTrap: Calling every pacemaker an absolute MRI contraindication—or choosing MRI just because it has no radiation when CT is the time-critical test.
oneLinePearl: MRI is a tissue-characterization tool, not a universal upgrade from CT.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Radiologists Referral Guidelines
CAR 2026 Recommendation for Safe MRI Use During Pregnancy
